articles.title: Mother demands answers, weeks after black woman found hanging from Mississippi tree
articles.summary: Her demands for information about what happened to Tasia Fortune have been echoed by shocked locals.
articles.body:
The mother of a black woman whose body was found hanging from a tree in Jackson, Mississippi, has told the BBC she is still waiting for answers from officials more than a month later.

Her demands have been echoed by a community in the southern US state that has been left shocked and angry.

After weeks of silence, police on Tuesday confirmed for the first time that they were investigating the death of Tasia Fortune, 29, as a potential homicide - while clarifying that her official cause of death has yet to be confirmed.

Authorities discovered Fortune's body on 3 August, hanging from a tree in the lot of an abandoned home.

Local concern over her death has been heightened by the fact that the state has a dark history of racial violence and lynchings.

The majority-black city has been left on edge. As the question lingers as to how Fortune died, petitions online signed by tens of thousands of people have called for more transparency, and members of US Congress have asked for federal intervention.

"It's making me angry," Fortune's mother, Christy Spivey, said. "What is the hold up?"

Spivey described desperate attempts to understand the status of the investigation and how multiple enquiries to police had gone unanswered.

The first update she had received from authorities in weeks came in a public city meeting on Tuesday evening as Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney discussed the case and said the department "has been investigating this case from day one as a homicide".

Brackney, in a statement to the BBC, elaborated and said the department always treats any pending death case as a "potential homicide" so that crucial evidence is not lost as police wait on autopsy results.

The department, though, had only previously described the case as a death investigation.

Tuesday's statement from Brackney said "we are conducting the investigation at the highest appropriate level while we await the medical examiner's findings", which would include an official cause and manner of death.

The medical examiner's office said it would not comment on the pending case.

Spivey last saw her daughter alive on 26 July, when Fortune had travelled from Mississippi, where she had lived for roughly the last decade, to Kentucky, where Spivey lives, for a family reunion.

The next time she saw her daughter - in a funeral home, days before her burial - she could barely look at her body.

"I didn't look straight at her. Her daddy did," she said. "I kind of looked from the side."

Spivey remembered their last conversation. "She was talking about, you know, maybe even coming home," she explained.

Fortune's death has left the community concerned that racial violence in Mississippi could be on the rise again. And in the absence of concrete details about the case, their suspicions are left to fester.

Fortune's death was the third incident in Mississippi in less than a year where police found someone dead and hanged from a tree.

The other two bodies - one black male, one white - were discovered in September 2025, on the exact same day.

Both were ruled a suicide, though the mother of one of the deceased - Trey Reed - contests those findings.

Fed-up residents have launched an online petition, which has gathered more than 50,000 signatures, for an independent investigation into the state's chief medical examiner, Dr Staci Turner, over the handling of a recent spate of cases involving people of colour. Another petition asks for the FBI to launch an investigation into Fortune's death

Jackson City Councilman Kenneth Stokes has also expressed concerns about the police investigation, saying he'd been outside the home where Fortune was thought to have lived multiple times and has never seen officers.

"All cases are important, but this one - a hanging in Mississippi - should rise to the top of the food chain," Stokes said.

He told the BBC he sent letters to both federal prosecutors at the Mississippi US attorney's office and the FBI weeks ago, urging that the investigation was "in dire need of assistance". He has yet to hear back from either.

"Nothing from nobody," Stokes said. "It's like nobody cares."

The BBC has reached out to the Mississippi US attorney's office and the local FBI office for comment.

US Congresswoman Jasmine Crockett has similarly requested federal intervention. In a letter to the US Department of Justice, she asked for an investigation into recent deaths in Mississippi - including that of Tasia Fortune - calling them "possible cases of modern-day lynchings". She cited the state's "appalling historical reputation of violent terrorism against black Americans".

In addition to Mississippi, there have been multiple other cases nationally of black Americans found hanged from trees, including four in North Carolina this year alone. Three were ruled a suicide. An autopsy is pending for the fourth death.

The BBC has reached out to the justice department for comment.

Stokes is clear that he does not know whether Fortune's death was a lynching, or whether race played a part at all. Nor does he care. He just wants answers.

Brandon King, president of the student National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) chapter at nearby Jackson State University, said the mystery of Fortune's death, combined with minimal updates from police, has led him and others to be "extra cautious" around campus.

The feeling, King said, was that "hey, you could be next. This is in Jackson. This is in your backyard".

The thought is extra worrying, he continued, because "this is supposed to be the capital. This is where I'm supposed to feel the most safe".

As for Spivey, she cried before heading to a funeral home for her daughter, dreading having to fill out a death certificate and decide whether to cremate or bury her firstborn child.

She wanted to cremate her daughter but decided, in the end, for a burial. She said she was holding out hope there would be updates in the investigation, which might mean needing to exhume her corpse.

articles.title: Wife of man killed when Amazon-branded plane overran runway files wrongful death lawsuit
articles.summary: The wife of one of the victims killed when an Amazon-branded plane overran a runway at a Miami airport, striking an airline cleaning service van and a passenger SUV, has filed a wrongful death lawsuit.
articles.body: The wife of one of the victims killed when an Amazon-branded plane overran a runway at a Miami airport, striking an airline cleaning service van and a passenger SUV, has filed a wrongful death lawsuit. Yaraisi Santiso Morejon, the wife of Yoel Rodriguez Naranjo, filed the lawsuit Wednesday, three days after the fatal incident at Miami International Airport that left four others dead and five injured. The lawsuit, which names Amazon, Amazon Air Cargo and the cargo airline 21 Air as defendants, alleges that the crash was a “foreseeable and preventable result of multiple, concurrent failures.” The plane’s two pilots, who survived the crash, Joseph Carroll and Jaime Felipe Silva Molina, are also listed as defendants. The suit accuses them of attempting a “high-speed, tailwind-affected landing” and cites pilot error and inadequate training. The Boeing 767-300 aircraft was on its third trip Sunday when it landed and then overran the runway, National Transportation Safety Board Chair Jennifer Homendy said. Earlier in the day, the plane had traveled from Cincinnati to Miami, and then Miami to San Juan, Puerto Rico. It was returning from San Juan when it crashed. An Amazon spokesperson previously said that the flight was operated by 21 Air. Homendy said that during the aircraft’s landing, it overran the runway and struck navigational aids and equipment before hitting a Ford van on airport property that was owned by Professional Ocean Service Corp., a contract cleaning service for airline companies. The plane careened through a perimeter fence and struck a Toyota SUV that was driving on a road nearby. The aircraft continued into the grass, where it hit a fence line that separated an area where Tesla robotaxis were stationed, Homendy said. Morejon’s attorneys said that Rodriguez Naranjo, 53, who was driving the van, died on impact. The workers were leaving their last job and were headed home when the crash occurred, attorney Mike Morgan said at a Wednesday news conference. Four of his colleagues were also killed. They were identified Tuesday by the Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office as Rolando Aleman Leon, 55; Julio C. Pineda, 75; Carlos Acosta Fajardo, 53; and Javierkys Reyes Quevedo, 47. The cleaning company said in a statement Tuesday that it was “heartbroken” by the deaths of its workers. One of Leon’s neighbors said he was very kind and would help take her to appointments. A family member said Leon’s son was devastated. A neighbor of Pineda remembered him as jovial and kind, and said he was known as “El mago,” or “The Magician,” because he was always doing magic tricks. “He was someone who was always laughing and telling stories,” Alberto Leandro said. “You’d see him and he’d crack a joke in the elevator.” Fellow neighbor Elana Forte said Pineda was “always calm” and “always laughing.” The law firm representing Acosta Fajardo’s family said he was “an incredible human being, a loving husband, devoted son, cherished friend, and valued co-worker.” Attorney Jorge P. Gutierrez Jr. said they will conduct a thorough and independent investigation into what happened. Five other people were injured and taken to the hospital. Eugenio Corredor, 79, and Ridoel Averhoff Diaz, 32, remain in critical condition, and Roosevelt Sebastian Perdomo Torres, 36, is stable, the Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office said Tuesday. Silva Molina, 37, and Carroll, 55, the two pilots, were treated and released. They could not be reached at phone numbers listed for them. Morgan said that it appears the pilots “grossly overshot” the runway. He said that based on the information that they have and their own research, the landing spot was overshot “by over 1,000 feet.” Morgan also accused the pilots of approaching the runway “grossly over the speed that they should have been attempting.” He said a “tailwind event” also made the landing more hazardous. “This aircraft should have made a fly-around attempt, a go-around attempt,” he said. The attorney also said that what they heard from the cockpit sounded “like a lot of confusion.” “It sounds as if there is an unknowing of what to do and unknowing of the imminent danger of overshooting the runway,” he said. 21 Air did not immediately respond to a request for comment. A spokesperson for Amazon and Amazon Air Cargo said in an updated statement Wednesday that its “deepest sympathies remain with the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating tragedy.” Amazon said it is fully cooperating with the investigation and will “continue to coordinate with 21 Air.” It also said that it has been working with officials in Miami-Dade to obtain contact information for the families affected by the crash. Homendy said at a news conference Tuesday night that Carroll, the captain, had 7,145 hours of flight experience, according to his March 31 medical. Silva Molina, the first officer, had logged 2,655 hours as of his Aug. 13 medical, she said. Carroll was rated to fly the type of aircraft involved in the crash in May, while Silva Molina was rated to fly it in April 2025, Homendy said. The plane was carrying more than 32,000 pounds of cargo, mostly contact lenses, when it crashed. The cause of the crash remains under investigation. The NTSB’s investigator in charge of the probe, Chihoon Shin, said Tuesday that the aircraft’s flight data recorder showed its thrust increased during landing in a way that was consistent with a “go-around” attempt, a maneuver in which a plane aborts its landing by pulling up and circling around to try to land again. Four seconds later, the throttles were reduced to idle power, and the landing gear brakes were reapplied, he said. Throttles were kept at idle, and the brakes remained applied until the end of the recording, Shin said, noting that “the speed brakes and the thrust reversers were not deployed.” Speed brakes are active flaps commonly deployed to help an aircraft slow down. Thrust reversers are typically used on passenger jets upon landing, also to help it slow down. Shin said it was way too soon to know why the speed brakes and thrust reversers weren’t deployed.

articles.title: Jeremy Corbyn finds a buyer for North London home at £700,000 after 19 years; former Labour leader bought Finsbury Park house for £363,000 in 2007 after initially listing it for £800,000
articles.summary: News News: Former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn is set to nearly double his money on his North London home after agreeing terms with a prospective buyer. According.
articles.body: Former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn is set to nearly double his money on his North London home after agreeing terms with a prospective buyer. According to The Telegraph, the 77-year-old Your Party MP for Islington North has put his three-bedroom terraced house in Finsbury Park on the market for offers over £700,000, after initially listing the property for £800,000 earlier this year.Corbyn bought the property for £363,000 in 2007 and has lived there for nearly two decades. The publication reported that the property is now under offer, although the final sale price has not yet been disclosed and will only become public once contracts have been exchanged.Jeremy Corbyn’s house price and sale historyThe North London property was initially listed in March by estate agent Kinleigh Folkard & Hayward with an asking price of £800,000. After failing to sell, the price was reduced to £780,000 in April and then to £750,000 in May before eventually being marketed for offers over £700,000.Corbyn had previously attempted to sell the same Islington property for almost £1 million in 2023, according to the report, but the sale did not go through.If the current deal is completed at around £700,000, Corbyn would have gained almost £337,000 on his original £363,000 purchase price - an increase of nearly 93 per cent.Inside Jeremy Corbyn’s three-bedroom townhouseThe “charming and spacious” three-storey terraced house features three double bedrooms, two reception rooms and a 26ft rear garden.The property listing describes the house as being on a quiet street close to Seven Sisters and Holloway Road. It is also within walking distance of Finsbury Park, Underground and Overground stations, with transport links to the City and West End.Photographs of the property show artwork and political-themed decorations, including a piece featuring the slogan “Peace: Build a Bridge Not A Wall” and a stylised image featuring numerous red flags.Inside the living room, the property has three packed bookshelves alongside a dining table.Jeremy Corbyn’s ‘dream street’ in IslingtonCorbyn previously described the street as his “dream street”, praising its friendly and mixed community.During his time as Labour leader from 2015 to 2020, the property became familiar to television audiences, with Corbyn frequently seen leaving the address while facing questions from journalists and members of the public.Neighbours on the street are understood to include supporters of the veteran left-wing politician. One neighbour previously described Corbyn as “very nice”.Corbyn has lived at the property with his wife, Laura Alvarez, a Mexican businesswoman and fair-trade coffee importer.How much council tax does Jeremy Corbyn pay?The property is in Council Tax Band E and would have attracted an annual bill of £2,577 this year, according to the property details reported by The Telegraph.Its Energy Performance Certificate gives the house a D rating. The property has gas heating and a gas boiler rather than a heat pump.Jeremy Corbyn’s gardening passion and property controversiesCorbyn has maintained an allotment in North London for more than two decades. During his time as Labour leader, he said gardening helped him become a better politician because it “helps you think about things and understand the natural process”.The Islington property has also been at the centre of several controversies. In 2018, Corbyn and Alvarez were refused planning permission to extend the front of the house.A year later, eco-activists glued their hands and chained themselves to Corbyn’s garden fence using a bike lock during a protest calling on him to declare a “climate emergency”.During his time as Labour leader, Corbyn was also reported to have installed mirrored glass in windows facing the street to prevent passers-by from looking into his living room.Corbyn, who was first elected to Parliament in 1983, served as Labour Party leader between 2015 and 2020. He later founded the left-wing Your Party and remains the MP for Islington North.The sale of his long-time North London home comes after almost two decades at the property. At an asking price of £700,000, the house is worth significantly more than the average property in England and is also above the reported London average.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: A couple bought a cabin overlooking a Tennessee river; nearly 20 years later, they protected the land forever
articles.summary: US News: Dan and Zita Elrod bought a wooded property overlooking Tennessee’s Duck River nearly 20-years-ago, hoping to find a peaceful escape from city life. I.
articles.body: Dan and Zita Elrod bought a wooded property overlooking Tennessee’s Duck River nearly 20-years-ago, hoping to find a peaceful escape from city life. In 2025, the couple made another important decision about the property, placing nearly 42 acres under a conservation easement designed to protect the land from intensive development and division of property into small plots. Their choice became part of a wider year of conservation across Tennessee, where private landowners, charities and public agencies worked together to safeguard thousands of acres. The Elrods’ story shows how personal attachment to a land can eventually become a commitment to protecting it for the future.How a couple protected their Tennessee river cabin for the futureThe Elrods had been looking for a quiet retreat when they first came across the property overlooking the Duck River. The wooded land and cabin offered the kind of setting they wanted, and the sight of an eagle during their first visit helped convince them that they had found the right place.Nearly 20 years later, they decided to ensure that its status would remain protected long after their own time there. According to the Tennessee Lookout, the couple entered into a conservation easement with The Land Trust for Tennessee in 2025.A conservation easement is a voluntary legal agreement between a landowner and a conservation organisation. It places permanent restrictions on certain future uses of a property in order to protect its natural or agricultural value.For the Elrods, this means their roughly 42 acres can remain centred around the cabin and surrounding forest. The protection also continues if the land is eventually sold or passed down to family members. Dan Elrod described the decision as a rare opportunity to do something permanent.The agreement was designed around the landowners’ wishesAccording to the Tennessee Lookout, conservation easements are not identical from one property to another. The restrictions are developed with the individual land and its owners in mind.Some agreements may prevent intensive development, such as dividing a property into a large number of housing plots. However, other activities can still be allowed. Farming, agricultural buildings and timber harvesting may remain possible when they fit the terms of the agreement and appropriate land management practices.This flexibility was important to the Elrods. Dan Elrod said landowners may have more options than they initially realise when considering an easement.The couple also did not give up ownership of their property. They can continue to own it, sell it or leave it to their heirs. What changes is that the conservation agreement remains attached to the land, meaning future owners must also follow its conditions.Why was protecting this land part of a bigger Tennessee effortThe Elrods’ decision was one small part of a much wider conservation effort across Tennessee during 2025. The Tennessee Lookout reported that TennGreen Land Conservancy preserved roughly 3,200 acres during the year through a mixture of conservation easements and land purchases. Meanwhile, The Land Trust for Tennessee conserved just under 1,000 acres with private landowners, mainly in Middle Tennessee.The properties involved were not all the same. Together, they included forests, rivers, pastures, waterfalls and habitats that support rare, threatened or endangered species.One of the year's largest conservation successes involved more than 7,400 acres of bottomland hardwood forest along the Hatchie River in West Tennessee. Multiple land trusts, non-profits and government agencies had worked for years to secure the property, which is now a wildlife management area.Conservation easements can protect land without taking it awayFor many landowners, the possibility of losing control over their property can be a major concern. Conservation groups therefore work with owners to determine whether an easement is suitable for the land and the future they want for it.The Land Trust for Tennessee received more than 400 enquiries about conservation easements in 2025, as reported by Tennessee Lookout. The organisation considers factors including farmland, water quality, wildlife habitat, scenic value and historic features when assessing potential projects.Once an agreement has been completed, the relationship does not simply end. The land trust continues to monitor the property and checks that the agreed conservation conditions are being maintained.The Land Trust for Tennessee has conserved roughly 137,000 acres through more than 460 conservation easements since its founding in 1999. If an organisation holding an easement were ever unable to continue its role, the agreement could legally be transferred to another organisation so that the land's protection could continue.New funding could help more Tennessee landownersCreating a conservation easement can involve costs, including land surveys, property appraisals and legal services. Although some landowners may qualify for tax benefits, those initial expenses can still discourage people from pursuing permanent protection.That could change for more Tennessee landowners through the Farmland Preservation Act, passed by the Tennessee General Assembly in 2025. According to the Tennessee Lookout, the law set aside $25 million for grants aimed at farmland and forest owners who place their land under conservation easements.Conservation groups hope the funding will make it easier for farmers and other landowners to protect properties that might otherwise face future development pressures.The Elrods' nearly 42-acre property is part of a much larger picture. What began with a search for a peaceful cabin beside the Duck River eventually became a decision to preserve a landscape beyond their own ownership. Nearly 20 years after they first spotted an eagle from the porch, the forest surrounding their retreat now has a form of protection intended to last for generations.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Inside Israel’s prisons, where Ben-Gvir’s cruelty is policy
articles.summary: Palestinian prisoners are being kept in inhumane conditions in Israeli detention facilities, overseen by Ben-Gvir.
articles.body:
When Palestinian photojournalist and former prisoner Muath Amarneh saw Israel’s National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’ s videos gloating over the decrepit conditions endured by imprisoned Palestinians, he thought of what happened before and after the cameras started rolling.

“When a figure like that comes to the prisons, they don’t show everything. What they do show is only certain video clips where the arrogance of that figure comes through,” Amarneh told Al Jazeera.

“But before and after, the prisoner is subjected to humiliation and beatings they don’t show the public. That whole hour of humiliation, they show half a minute of it, or a minute, or two minutes.”

Ben-Gvir, who oversees Israel’s prison system in his role, has spent recent weeks broadcasting what he views as his accomplishments in office.

An AI-generated video posted to his social media in August showed well-fed Palestinian men on a conveyor belt entering a detention facility, then emerging emaciated, weeping – captioned “We promised, we delivered”. He deleted it as comparisons to Nazi concentration camps mounted.

Days later, he posted footage of himself confronting female prisoners. One told him she had not showered in three days and was not receiving medical treatment. “The good conditions in the prisons are over,” Ben-Gvir told her. “I am directly responsible for everything. I am pleased with these conditions.”

Detainees’ testimonies and data from Palestinian rights groups offer a glimpse of what that policy has meant inside Israeli prisons.

Amarneh, 39, who now lives in the Dheisheh refugee camp south of Bethlehem, has been arrested twice since the genocidal war on Gaza began, both times under administrative detention.

There are now roughly 3,200 administrative detainees – more than double the approximately 1,300 held before October 7, 2023, according to Addameer, a Palestinian prisoners’ advocacy group.

Israel and the United States accuse Addameer of supporting “terrorism”, a charge the group denies, and Amarneh’s numerous run-ins with Israeli forces started when he began work as a photojournalist.

In 2019, Israeli forces shot him with a rubber-coated metal bullet while he was covering Israeli attacks near Hebron and wearing a press vest. A bullet took out his left eye and left shrapnel lodged near his skull.

Amarneh was first taken into administrative detention in October 2023, a week after Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began, and was held for nine months in Megiddo and Nafha prisons.

After his release, he deliberately moved away from news work towards documentary work, hoping to reduce his risk of being imprisoned again.

Nevertheless, he was arrested again in August 2025 and held for eight months at Ofer prison, still without charge. “My charge was working in media,” he said.

Sahar Francis, a lawyer who was the executive director of Addameer, said Ben-Gvir’s nearly four-year tenure as minister responsible for the prison authority did not create the system’s cruelty so much as intensify it. “From his first day overseeing the prison authority, he closed the only two bakeries producing bread for detainees.”

“Then came October 7, after which the situation in prisons worsened considerably. Family visits and Red Cross access were suspended, while lawyers were barred for the first four or five months. Clothing, food and books were confiscated, leaving detainees with a single change of clothes,” she added.

Amarneh wore the same trousers for 90 days. Health clinics were shuttered. Special units began raiding sections daily, beating detainees – a practice she says has caused multiple deaths in custody.

“They were always using torture. But what happened after the genocide is that they came back to conditions similar to the early years of the occupation, on the level of the brutality, the physical abuse, the rape, the harassment,” said Francis.

Across his two periods of administrative detention, Amarneh lost 35kg (77 pounds) over nine months.

“I lived through the transformation of the prisons – how they were before the war and how they became,” said Amarneh. “The prisons, where life was already hard to begin with, were transformed into places where life became impossible: a place that isn’t fit for human life.”

By the time of his second arrest in 2025, Amarneh said, he noticed deteriorating conditions in detention facilities.

“I never imagined the situation would be worse than the times before. The scale of the humiliation in there was enormous, to an indescribable degree,” he said.

Amarneh was stripped of his prescription glasses for six months, and others were deprived of regular access to showers and basic hygiene products. When detainees managed to have a rare shower, they were forced to sit out in the rain immediately afterwards. Prison guards regularly referred to Amarneh and others as animals and cursed their mothers and wives. Often, guards remarked they “should have just killed you”.

He remembers guards forbidding prisoners to stand in the sun, telling them “this sun is ours, not yours”. When one detainee simply asked when Eid was taking place, a riot unit stormed into the cell 10 minutes later, beat everyone else inside, and shot the questioner with rubber bullets, “so you won’t dare ask about Eid again”.

To make matters worse, Amarneh’s wife was pregnant while he was held in Ofer prison, with no information about her condition. He only happened to learn by chance later from a lawyer visiting another detainee in his section that his wife had given birth and only found out the child’s name, Osama, two months later.

Blankets were forbidden between 5am and 4pm, through the coldest months, leaving the prisoners “the colour of a dead body”, he said.

Medical care was all but nonexistent, with one person given the wrong diabetes medication at the wrong dose.

When an infection in his leg left Amarneh partly paralysed, he was given minimal treatment only after his lawyer noticed his condition at a court hearing. Later, his eye implant became dislodged after a wound reopened, but prison authorities denied him a hospital transfer, saying his condition was “not seriously dangerous”.

“That’s it, I’m going to die here,” he remembered thinking. When the pain from the beatings and infections became unbearable, guards offered a single painkiller tablet to be divided among 11 detainees.

The United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention ruled in 2024 that Amarneh’s first detention was unlawful and discriminatory. Press freedom organisations have also raised his repeated imprisonment as part of a broader pattern targeting Palestinian journalists. But none of it stopped his second arrest, 10 months later.

Francis said international bodies like the UN’s Working Group “don’t have the power to impose their decisions on the Israeli side”.

“At the end, it’s an opinion — a decision that needs more political will in order to be implemented,” she added.

She sees the same double standard in international accountability: cases of torture under Syria’s Bashar al-Assad regime have been prosecuted in Germany and France against officers and interrogators, “where in our case we always fail. It’s open for other cases, but not for Palestinians.”

‘I am directly responsible for everything’

Francis believes Ben-Gvir’s on-camera boasts that “I am directly responsible for everything” could be relevant to any potential case against him in the International Criminal Court (ICC).

“Such a person – a political figure, a minister – is at the top of the pyramid of decision-making,” she said. “If they are not using these tools against people like Ben-Gvir, then where?”

Al Jazeera has reached out to Ben-Gvir, the Israeli National Security ministry, and the Israeli military for comment, but has not received a response.

Before Amarneh left prison the second time, officers said they were going to monitor what he writes. “If you want to come back to prison, go ahead,” they told him.

A few months after his April release, Amarneh rarely leaves his house in the Dheisheh camp, fearing arrest.

“For me, being in prison is easier than being outside prison. The psychological pressure I’m living with is equivalent to being imprisoned again,” he said. “When you’re in prison, that’s it – you know you’re in prison, you know the situation you’re in. But on the outside, I’m under enormous psychological pressure.”

So, what is Ben-Gvir’s aim in implementing such inhumane treatment in detention facilities?

“He wants the land without the people. But we’re here. Either I die here, or I live here,” said Amarneh. “I’m not a terrorist. I don’t thirst for violence or blood or anything like that. On the contrary, I want to live in peace. But he doesn’t want that. He doesn’t even want us to live.”

articles.title: Google to fund Finnish AI with €13bn investment and nuclear power pact
articles.summary: The US tech giant says the €13bn data centre project will create tens of thousands of jobs.
articles.body:
Google will buy up to half the electricity produced by one of Finland's nuclear power plants as part of a record €13bn (£11bn; $15bn) investment in the country's AI infrastructure, the company announced.

The US tech giant said the package would fund three new data centres, expand an existing site and support energy projects to power growing demand for AI services.

"This is Google's largest single investment in Europe and a testament to Finland's leadership in responsibly building AI infrastructure," the company said on Wednesday.

"Google's decision is a clear testament to our strengths," Finland's Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said in a statement.

As part of the deal, Google signed a 22-year contract with Finnish utility Fortum to buy up to 50% of the output from the Loviisa nuclear power plant.

Earlier this week, TikTok announced a $1bn investment in Finland to build a new data centre in Kouvola, pointing to the country's "strong digital infrastructure, clean energy mix, robust data governance and skilled tech talent".

Finland has emerged as an attractive location for data centres because of its cool climate, plentiful low-carbon electricity and relatively uncongested power grid. The colder temperatures can reduce the energy needed to cool facilities packed with computer servers.

Technology companies are racing to secure power supplies as the AI boom drives demand for vast networks of data centres.

The Google investment is expected to support more than 37,000 jobs during construction and boost Finland's GDP by €3.6bn a year, according to Google. Construction is set to take place in 2027 and 2028.

"The value of the data economy extends far beyond direct investment into spurring innovation, research and development," Orpo added.

"Deepening our collaboration with Google will deliver lasting benefits for both parties."

Google will build new data centres in Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala, while expanding its existing facility in Hamina, which it established after converting a former paper mill in 2009.

The infrastructure will help support products such as its AI chatbot Gemini, alongside services including Search, Maps and YouTube.

Google said the investments also covered "clean energy projects, and dedicated nature and community funds to support local biodiversity, education, research, and workforce development".

"Google is proud to deepen our roots in Finland," said Ruth Porat, president and chief investment officer of Alphabet and Google.

"This investment underscores Google's commitment to grow our presence responsibly, pairing the expansion of our technical infrastructure with new energy capacity, grid enhancements, and energy affordability initiatives," she added.

Earlier this year, Google's parent company Alphabet raised its global spending plans to as much as $205bn as it sought to expand computing capacity for AI services.

The agreement with Fortum provides long-term financial certainty for the Loviisa plant, which currently generates about 10% of Finland's electricity.

Fortum said Google's commitment would support an investment programme aimed at extending the life of the nuclear station and increasing its generating capacity.

articles.title: Andrew, Tristan Tate denied bail as UK extradition fight continues
articles.summary: US News: Social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate were denied bail on Wednesday by a US court as they fight extradition to Britain, where they are want.
articles.body: Social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate were denied bail on Wednesday by a US court as they fight extradition to Britain, where they are wanted over rape and other charges.Magistrate Judge Lauren Louis denied the brothers’ request for release from a Miami jail following a hearing last month in federal court.Andrew Tate, 39, and Tristan Tate, 38, were arrested in Miami on July 18 after Britain sought their extradition. They face charges including rape, assault and facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation. The brothers, who hold both US and British citizenship, have denied any wrongdoing.US prosecutors argued that the brothers should remain in custody, citing the presumption of detention in international extradition cases. They said the Tates could pose a danger to the community and could attempt to flee.Prosecutors also cited allegations from British authorities that the brothers strangled victims during alleged rapes. They pointed to separate human trafficking cases in Romania, where authorities have alleged that the brothers tried to influence witnesses while under judicial supervision.The defence rejected the arguments for continued detention. Lawyers said the brothers’ "extraordinary public visibility" would make it difficult for them to flee and argued that they had complied with court proceedings in Romania.The lawyers had proposed releasing the brothers on bond, with conditions including surrendering their passports and wearing location-monitoring devices.The extradition process could take months. Britain has until September 16 to submit its full extradition request to the US State Department, according to US court records.The latest arrests followed new charges brought by Britain's Crown Prosecution Service over alleged offences involving four victims between July 2010 and August 2017.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Apple announces new iPhones in first event under  CEO John Ternus
articles.summary: Apple began its flagship product announcement with the new iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, highlighting its AI capabilities. It’s expected that the company will also announce a foldable phone.
articles.body: Apple opened its annual fall product event on Wednesday with a series of iPhone updates, the first launch presentation led by John Ternus since he took over as CEO from Tim Cook on Sept. 1 — and the company is expected to use the event to unveil its first foldable iPhone, its biggest change to the device since it was introduced in 2007. Apple has not confirmed the foldable device, and details including its name, price and release date were not known as of publication. Beginning the livestreamed event at the company’s Cupertino, California, headquarters, Ternus and other employees announced the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, which includes incremental changes to the product lines like new colors and a new ability to customize the voice of its Siri artificial intelligence assistant. The company highlighted increased battery capabilities in the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, which it says charges faster than previous generations and has over 24 hours of battery life. Other changes include a feature called “Apple Reference Image,” which the company said could be used to prove the authenticity of an image in an era when AI-generated content is becoming ubiquitous. The company also said it was improving the aperture control on the iPhone camera and the device’s thermal management, which is designed to prevent overheating. Ternus inherits a company facing increasingly serious competition in phones and pressure to show that it can still drive the upgrade cycles that made the iPhone the most profitable product in consumer electronics. A foldable iPhone would be Apple’s first genuinely new iPhone form factor in nearly two decades. The appeal of the devices is often about their size — some foldable phones expand to be as large as a tablet, while others are marketed for how compact they are when they fold up. Apple is known for launching products into existing markets and quickly taking over market share, as it did with wireless headphones and smartwatches. Samsung has cornered the foldable phone market since 2019, building niche demand for the product that shipped 19.6 million units in 2025, just a fraction of overall smartphone sales. On Monday, Chinese tech companies Huawei and Xiaomi launched their own foldable phones, priced at $2,980 and $3,725, respectively. Fans of foldable devices have worked to attract converts and dispel consumers’ potential concerns, including about durability: If it can fold, does that mean it can break more easily? Livestream videos posted online claim to show users folding some devices 200,000 times. So far, though, foldable phones have struggled to break through to a major success in the mobile market. The idea of a flexible display has been around for decades. In 2007, the same year Apple introduced the iPhone, a company called Polymer Vision released a prototype of a foldable e-reader called Readius with a grayscale display. The company shuttered in 2009. articles.title: South Korea built an underground seed vault to save wild plants but some seeds could help crops survive a hotter, harsher future
articles.summary: Rest of World News: As climate change accelerates biodiversity loss and threatens food security, South Korea is expanding an unusual form of protection, preserving the ge.
articles.body: As climate change accelerates biodiversity loss and threatens food security, South Korea is expanding an unusual form of protection, preserving the genetic resources of wild plants for the future. At the centre of this effort is the Baekdudaegan Global Seed Vault, operated by the Korea Arboreta and Gardens Institute (KoAGI). The underground facility in Bonghwa, North Gyeongsang Province, permanently stores wild plant seeds as insurance against natural disasters, environmental destruction and species extinction. KoAGI President Shim Sang-taek has outlined plans to strengthen international cooperation, conserve crop wild relatives and support countries particularly vulnerable to climate change. The vault currently holds around 290,000 seed accessions, including approximately 131,000 from outside Korea. Its growing international role reflects a changing approach to conservation, safeguarding biodiversity is not simply about protecting species today, but preserving genetic resources that could help future ecosystems and food systems withstand a hotter and increasingly unpredictable world.Why is Korea’s global seed vault important for the climate crisisThe Baekdudaegan Global Seed Vault is designed to protect wild plant genetic resources from threats that could permanently destroy them. Climate change is increasing pressure on ecosystems while natural disasters, habitat destruction and species extinction create additional risks. By storing seeds underground, the facility provides a long-term safety net for plant diversity. The vault currently contains around 290,000 seed accessions, with approximately 131,000 originating outside Korea. KoAGI sees the facility as more than a storage site, aiming to develop it into an international platform for biodiversity conservation. The strategy is based on cooperation between countries, research organisations and governments because plant genetic resources can have value far beyond the places where they were originally collected. Preserving them now means keeping biological resources available for future generations.How could wild plants protect future food security?A major part of KoAGI’s work focuses on crop wild relatives, or CWRs, wild plants that are genetically related to cultivated crops. Unlike modern crops, which have often been bred for consistent yields and particular characteristics, their wild relatives can carry traits that allow them to survive difficult conditions. These may include tolerance to drought, salinity, disease and extreme temperatures. Such characteristics could become increasingly important as climate change alters agricultural conditions and exposes crops to new environmental pressures. Working with a consortium of eight universities, the institute secures an average of 300 genetic-resource samples from around 30 species each year, and has compiled more than 7,100 data points on characteristics including drought tolerance, salt tolerance, disease resistance and potential antioxidant or anti-inflammatory properties.How is Korea building a global seed safety net?KoAGI is extending the role of the Baekdudaegan Global Seed Vault beyond South Korea through international partnerships. Its network has grown from 38 participating institutions to 58, with cooperation involving Botanic Gardens Conservation International and a pilot project focused on small island developing states. These countries can be particularly exposed to rising sea levels, extreme weather and habitat loss, while some lack the infrastructure or expertise needed for long-term seed conservation. Through the “Island Seeds, Global Legacy” initiative, KoAGI provides training, equipment and operational support for collecting and storing wild plant seeds. The collected material is divided between the originating country's seed bank and the Korean vault. This creates duplicate collections, reducing the possibility that one disaster could destroy irreplaceable genetic resources. Participating countries also retain sovereign rights over their deposited seeds.Why is Korea changing how ecosystem restoration is measured?KoAGI is also challenging the way restoration projects are judged. Instead of simply counting trees planted or measuring the area covered by a project, the institute wants to determine whether ecosystems and biodiversity have genuinely recovered. It has been registered as Korea’s certification hub for the Global Biodiversity Standard, which evaluates whether restoration creates measurable improvements in vegetation, habitats and species diversity. Its criteria include prioritising native species, protecting existing habitats, preventing invasive species and working with local communities. KoAGI plans to assess restoration projects, train professional evaluators and provide consulting based on international standards. The institute also operates SeedPedia, a public database containing more than 40,000 records covering 2,273 native plant species. The wider goal is to connect conservation, scientific research and practical restoration while providing evidence that nature-based projects are producing genuine ecological benefits.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Tate brothers denied bail by Miami judge as they fight extradition to U.K. on sex crime charges
articles.summary: A judge denied bail for Andrew and Tristan Tate, the “manosphere” influencers who’ll now have to remain behind bars in Florida while fighting extradition to the U.K. on dozens of sex crime charges.
articles.body: MIAMI — A federal judge on Wednesday denied bail for Andrew and Tristan Tate, the “manosphere” influencers who’ll now have to remain behind bars in Florida while fighting extradition to the United Kingdom on dozens of sex crime charges. The brothers failed to show they were not a flight risk, a danger to the community or deserved special consideration for bail, U.S. Magistrate Judge Lauren Louis ruled. “Based upon the foregoing, I find that Respondents have failed to meet their burden to demonstrate that they do not present a risk of flight or danger to the community, or that special circumstances warrant their release,” Louis wrote. “Respondents have failed to demonstrate that special circumstances here warrant relief.” Andrew and Tristan Tate have been charged with dozens of counts of rape, assault and sex trafficking in the United Kingdom. The brothers, who are dual U.K.-U.S. nationals, were taken into custody in Miami in July after prosecutors in the United Kingdom filed new charges against them. They are fighting extradition to that county. Their attorney, Joe McBride, has denied the allegations and said their incarceration was the “result of an unholy alliance between the enemies of free speech in the United States and the United Kingdom.” Prosecutors in the U.K. had argued against their release, saying in a filing earlier this month that their own statements suggest the brothers intended to evade justice. The filing also alleged they make seek to interfere with witnesses and said the brothers repeatedly sought the names of their accusers from prosecutors in exchange for a “security” fee worth tens of thousands of pounds and a promise not to publicly identify the accusers. The Crown Prosecution Service declined the offer in an effort to safeguard the complainants, the filing states. McBride said the filing “drips falsehood from every page.” A former professional kickboxer, Andrew Tate, 39, built a vast online following espousing misogynistic and hypermasculine views. He once told an interviewer that there was “no way you can be rooted in reality and not be sexist.” U.K. prosecutors previously charged the Tates with 21 counts of rape, assault occasioning actual bodily harm and arranging or facilitating travel for sexual exploitation. Andrew Tate was also charged with controlling prostitution. The additional charges filed last month against Andrew Tate include seven counts of rape, 15 counts of making/distributing indecent images of children and four counts of possession of extreme pornography. Tristan Tate, 38, was charged with six additional counts of rape, sexual assault and sexual exploitation charges. U.K authorities said the alleged crimes took place between 2010 and 2017. The brothers also face criminal charges in Romania, where they reportedly moved in 2016 to build an online porn business and were later indicted on allegations of forming an organized criminal group, human trafficking, trafficking of minors and money laundering. They have denied the charges. Juliette Arcodia reported from Miami and David K. Li from New York City.
